To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Rosetta de Novo method can assemble structures of multidomain protein from structures of isolated protein domains, and that the method is accurate enough to be useful for structure determination of proteins that are too large or too difficult to crystallize.
a new method was developed for predicting structures of multidomain protein from structures of individual domains.
the method can be applied to a wide range of proteins and that, when applied to proteins for which the structures are known, the method can predict the structures with very high accuracy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing methods for protein structure determination, prediction, and refinement.
the development and application of methods for predicting the structure of multidomain proteins.
the development of computational methods for protein structure prediction, and the application of these methods to a wide variety of biological systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this method can be used to predict the structure of a multidomain protein from its constituent domains with a high degree of confidence.

the method is a very useful tool for the structural analysis of multidomain proteins, which should be used in combination with experimental data, and that the method is not a panacea for the structural analysis and design of multidomain proteins.
this work represents a significant contribution to the field of protein modeling and that it will be of great interest and use to the protein modeling community.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is possible to predict the structure of a protein from its amino acid sequence, provided that the protein has already been crystallized.
the structures of multidomain protein assemblies can be predicted from the structures of their individual domains.
the method is able to predict the structure of the linker region with an accuracy of 0.8 Å RMSD and that the accuracy of the final structure is limited by the accuracy of the individual domains.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, with the current level of accuracy of de novo structure prediction, it is possible to use de novo prediction as an efficient and accurate means to assemble structures of multidomain and multi‐subunit proteins from their component domains.

, in many cases, a low‐resolution search is sufficient to find the correct conformation of the domain linker, and the high‐resolution search is then able to find the correct side chain conformations and to optimize the backbone conformations.

it is possible to use a combination of low‐resolution and high‐resolution searches to predict structures of multidomain protein assemblies with accuracy that is comparable to that of high‐resolution searches alone.
